description: We are an enthusiastic team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary: Your ship is falling apart, and the only way home is through space. Space Explorer is a browser game where you fly a damaged rocket to the Moon, Mars and the Sun, hunt down glowing ship parts, and fight off monsters, all to make it back to Earth alive. What makes it special is the science. Each planet uses its real gravity, so you feel it in the controls. On the Moon your ship floats and drifts, on Mars it handles normally, and near the Sun gravity drags you down so hard you have to fight to stay in the air. Real NASA facts appear along the way, like how a day on Mars lasts about 24 hours 40 minutes. Before launch you choose a rocket and spend a $100 budget on fuel. It runs in any browser with nothing to install, so anyone can play and learn in a few minutes.
details:
Space Explorer drops you into a race against a dying spaceship. Your ship is breaking down far from home, and the only way to save it is to visit three worlds, the Moon, Mars and the Sun, and find the parts that keep it flying. Then you have to get back to Earth.

Every planet is a level with its own surface, sky and monsters. On the Moon you cross grey dust and craters under a black sky, with Earth hanging above you. On Mars you fly over a rust red, dusty world. Near the Sun the sky burns orange and the ground glows with heat. Four glowing ship parts appear one at a time on each planet, each with its own name, like Fuel Pump or Reactor Core. You need any three of them, so there is always a spare. Monsters chase you the whole time, so you shoot them while watching your hull, your fuel and the clock.

The big idea is that you feel the science instead of just reading it. Each level uses the planet’s real gravity: 1.62 m/s² on the Moon, 3.71 on Mars and 274 near the Sun. On the Moon your ship floats and drifts and is hard to stop. On Mars it handles normally. Near the Sun, gravity pulls you down fast and slows you, so you have to keep thrusting up to stay alive. The level screens also share real NASA facts, such as the Moon’s gravity being about one sixth of Earth’s, a Mars day lasting about 24 hours 40 minutes, and the Sun’s surface reaching about 5,500 degrees Celsius.

Before launch, you plan like a real mission team. You pick a rocket (Scout, Cruiser or Titan) and spend a $100 budget on the rocket and extra fuel, so every choice has a trade off.

Why it matters: many students find space science hard to picture. A short game that lets you feel how gravity changes from world to world can make the numbers stick. There is nothing to install and no account to make, so it works for anyone with a laptop and a browser, in class or at home.

How we built it: HTML, JavaScript and the canvas for the graphics, the Web Audio API for sound effects, Google Fonts for text, and Netlify for hosting. Every planet, monster, rocket and sound is created in code, so the whole game loads fast from a single file.

What we thought about: keeping each level to around two minutes so players can finish a full mission in one sitting, keeping the controls simple (keyboard and mouse), making the ship parts impossible to miss, and keeping the science accurate while still making it fun. Our team’s space look guided the design of the screens.

Use of AI: the game’s code was written with help from an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic), following our concept, screen designs and instructions. This is stated on the game’s home screen, in the page metadata and on slide 6 of our presentation. The slides and these descriptions were also drafted with AI help. All graphics and sounds are generated by that code. We did not use AI generated images, video or audio files, and we did not use any NASA logos or branding
